blocks.purpose: Defines what a style guide is with a bolded anchor sentence and prerequisite bullets, covering the core idea that style guides settle disputed rules.

data.anchor: A style guide is a reference book of agreed-upon choices that settles disputed usage questions — it tells writers which option to follow, even when the rules of English allow more than one.
prerequisites: Grammar gives you the hard rules: a sentence needs a subject and a verb, and words must fit together. Those are not debatable.
Usage is different: it covers choices like which word to pick or where to put a comma, where several options are grammatically possible.
Some word pairs get mixed up so often (affect and effect) that editors argue about them too — which makes them perfect examples of usage questions.
A fragment is an incomplete sentence and a run-on jams sentences together; both are errors, not style choices — knowing the difference matters later in this lesson.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side comparison of two real style guides (e.g., AP vs. Chicago) showing how they disagree on a specific disputed rule like the Oxford comma.

data.footnote: A style guide settles disputed usage by declaring a house choice — it does not discover the one true answer.

items.label: A set of choices
items.text: A decision manual for questions where two reasonable answers exist. It picks one so everyone in a newsroom, publishing house, or school writes the same way.
items.example: Chicago says: use the Oxford comma. AP says: leave it out.

items.label: Consistency
items.text: The main goal is not perfection — it is sameness. Readers should never notice the style flipping mid-article.

items.label: Changeable
items.text: Guides get revised every few years. When real-world usage shifts, the guide updates to match it.

rightColumn.heading: What a style guide is NOT

items.label: Not the grammar police
items.text: A style guide does not override hard grammar rules. No guide allows fragments or run-ons in formal writing.
items.example: "She went to the store. Because she was hungry." stays an error under every guide.

items.label: Not universal law
items.text: Two guides can give opposite answers to the same question, and both are correct within their own system. There is no Supreme Court of English.

items.label: Not eternal truth
items.text: A rule inside a guide can be dropped in the next edition. The guide follows usage; it does not command it.

blocks.purpose: Tells the short story of a real usage debate (e.g., split infinitives or singular 'they') that caused style guides to change, showing rules evolve over time.

beforeAfter.after: Editors slowly gave up. Chicago dropped its ban in 2014, and most guides now accept split infinitives when splitting sounds better. Usage had already changed — the rules followed.
beforeAfter.before: Style guides and teachers banned split infinitives for over a century. Careful writers contorted sentences to keep "to" and its verb together, often making them clunkier.

data.crisis: English grammar handbooks copied Latin patterns, and in Latin an infinitive is one word that cannot be split. So 19th-century editors declared that English infinitives must never be split either — a rule with no real basis in how English works.
story: The rule made famous by Star Trek's "to boldly go" — with "boldly" wedged inside the infinitive "to go" — had been attacked since the 1800s. Grammar writers insisted the adverb belonged before the whole phrase: "boldly to go."

But no English speaker actually talked that way. Famous writers kept splitting infinitives on purpose because the split version often sounds stronger and clearer. The ban survived mostly on habit and snobbery.
data.takeaway: When everyday usage and a rule collide for long enough, usage usually wins — style guides update, and yesterday's "error" becomes a choice.
data.title: The rule that took 150 years to die

blocks.purpose: Targets the #1 misconception — that disputed usage rules are always hard grammar errors rather than style choices — by presenting a tricky sentence and revealing why intuition fails.

choices: It is flat-out wrong because the serial comma is required in all sentences.
It is a style choice — either version is fine if you pick one style guide and follow it consistently.
It is a fragment error, since a comma can replace the word "and."
It is correct only if every comma in the whole document is removed.
data.commonErrorLabel: Treating style choices as hard errors
data.context: "I thanked my parents, Beyoncé and Batman." Does dropping the Oxford comma make this sentence an error?
data.correctReasoning: The sentence is grammatically complete either way. The Oxford comma is disputed usage: AP omits it, Chicago keeps it. The right move is to choose one guide and apply it consistently, not to call either version an error.
data.question: A student writes: "I thanked my parents, Beyoncé and Batman." Another student says the missing comma before "and" makes this a grammar error. What is the best judgment of that claim?
data.recoveryTip: Before flagging anything as an error, ask: does a major style guide actually allow this? If yes, it is a style choice — pick a guide and stay consistent.

trapReasons.0: This sounds like what strict teachers say, but no universal rule requires the serial comma — that is exactly why guides disagree.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: Your intuition screams that the missing comma causes real confusion, so it must be an error. But confusion is not the test for a grammar error — a broken grammar rule is. The sentence has a subject, a verb, and complete clauses either way. Comma placement before "and" is a disputed usage question, and reputable guides disagree about it, which is the whole definition of a style choice.

blocks.purpose: Compact key-value matrix summarizing major disputed rules, which style guides settle them, and how to check, for quick reference and retention.

rows.detail: It settles disputed usage for one group of writers; it does not rewrite grammar.
rows.value: A rulebook a publication or organization follows so its writing stays consistent.

rows.detail: AP drops it; Chicago keeps it. Both are right within their own system.
rows.value: The comma before "and" in a list — a style choice, not a required or forbidden mark.

rows.detail: Once banned, now accepted: Chicago dropped its ban in 2014, AP never enforced it strictly.
rows.value: Splitting "to" from its verb ("to boldly go") — widely accepted today.

rows.detail: AP accepted it in 2017; Chicago permits it. Real usage drove the change.
rows.value: Using "they" for one person of unknown or nonbinary gender — now accepted by major guides.

rows.detail: Once a banned "error"; now widely accepted when it is sincere.
rows.value: "Hopefully, it will snow" — long attacked, now standard in most guides.

rows.detail: Follow your assigned guide; if none is assigned, never mix them.
rows.value: Check whether a guide has been assigned; if not, pick one (AP or Chicago) and apply it consistently.

rows.detail: Effect = noun (the result). Affect = verb (to change). Ask: thing or action?
rows.value: Most often affect is the verb (to influence); effect is the noun (a result).

rows.detail: Fragments, run-ons, and broken agreement fail under every guide. Disputed commas and word choices do not.
rows.value: Real grammar errors break rules no guide allows; style choices are spots where guides disagree.
